# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** Louvain detects communities by repeatedly moving graph vertices into neighboring groups when the move increases modularity, then replacing each group by a coarse-grained vertex and repeating.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Biological question** | Which cells, samples, genes, or contigs form densely connected groups in a similarity or interaction graph? |
| **Computational problem** | Partition a large weighted graph into groups with more internal edge weight than expected under a degree-preserving null model |
| **Method type** | Greedy graph clustering and multilevel optimization |
| **Input** | An undirected weighted graph, commonly a [k-nearest-neighbor graph](k-nearest-neighbor-graphs.qmd) of cells |
| **Output** | A community label per vertex and a hierarchy of coarsened graphs |
| **Bioinformatics uses** | Cell-type/state discovery, gene co-expression modules, protein-interaction modules, and metagenomic graph exploration |
| **Prerequisites** | Weighted graphs, degree, null models, and [k-nearest-neighbor graphs](k-nearest-neighbor-graphs.qmd) |

# The objective: modularity

For an undirected weighted graph with edge weights $A_{ij}$, weighted degree $k_i=\sum_j A_{ij}$, and total edge weight $m=\tfrac12\sum_{ij}A_{ij}$, modularity of a partition $c$ is

$$
Q=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{ij}\left(A_{ij}-\gamma\frac{k_i k_j}{2m}\right)\mathbf{1}\{c_i=c_j\}.
$$

The first term rewards observed within-community edges. The second is the weight expected if edges were rewired at random while preserving vertex degrees. The resolution parameter $\gamma$ controls scale: increasing it generally favors smaller communities. Thus a community is not an intrinsic label hidden in the data; it is a partition preferred by a specific graph, null model, and resolution.

# How Louvain works

```text
weighted graph
  -> place every vertex in its own community
  -> greedily move each vertex to a neighboring community if modularity increases
  -> aggregate every resulting community into one weighted super-vertex
  -> repeat local moves and aggregation until modularity no longer improves
```

During a local-moving pass, Louvain considers only communities containing a neighbor of the current vertex. It evaluates the modularity gain of moving the vertex and selects a positive-gain move, in an implementation-dependent order. Once no individual move improves $Q$, all vertices in each community are contracted to a super-vertex. Edge weights between super-vertices are summed; internal edges become self-loops. A new pass on that smaller graph can expose a larger-scale improvement.

The method is fast because it uses local gain calculations and graph coarsening rather than enumerating all partitions. It is heuristic: reaching a high modularity score does not prove the global maximum was found.

# A small example

Imagine a cell graph with strong edges inside two groups and one weak cross-edge:

```text
A -- B -- C       D -- E -- F
      \             /
       -- weak edge --
```

Starting from singleton communities, moves that join $A$, $B$, and $C$ make more internal weight than expected and increase modularity; analogous moves join $D$, $E$, and $F$. Joining the two triples would include the weak bridge but lose the contrast between their dense internal connectivity and the null expectation, so it need not increase $Q$. In real data, edge weights and degree heterogeneity—not a drawing—determine the calculation.

# Using it for single-cell data

In a common workflow, normalize and quality-control the expression matrix, choose a feature representation such as principal components, construct a weighted cell-neighbor graph, then run Louvain at one or more declared resolutions. Software may also use shared-nearest-neighbor weights or a graph after batch-integration; those choices materially alter the result.

```text
counts and metadata
  -> QC, normalization, feature/PCA representation
  -> neighbor graph and edge weights
  -> Louvain at documented resolution(s) and seed(s)
  -> inspect markers, batches, donors, and stability
  -> annotate clusters using independent biological evidence
```

Community labels are identifiers, not cell types. Inspect marker genes, known controls, donor/batch composition, doublet scores, library size, and reproducibility across plausible graph and resolution settings. A visually separated [UMAP](umap-dimensionality-reduction.qmd) island is not by itself validation: UMAP coordinates are a visualization of graph structure, while Louvain directly optimizes an objective on the graph.

# Important limitations

| Issue | Consequence | Useful response |
|---|---|---|
| Resolution limit | Small dense groups can be merged when optimizing global modularity | Explore justified resolutions and validate small groups independently |
| Random order / ties | Different runs can return different high-scoring partitions | Fix and report seeds; compare partitions across runs |
| Graph construction | Neighbor count, representation, metric, and integration define the edges | Check stability over scientifically defensible preprocessing choices |
| Disconnected or poorly sampled states | A cluster may reflect sampling, batch, or graph fragmentation | Inspect connectivity and technical covariates before biological claims |
| Hierarchical outputs | Coarsening levels are not automatically biological levels | Select and justify a level rather than treating every level as ontology |

Modularity also has many near-optimal solutions, so one reported partition can conceal uncertainty. Perturbing cells, edges, donors, or preprocessing and quantifying agreement is more informative than treating a single label vector as definitive.

# Louvain and related methods

Louvain is a natural follow-on to [k-nearest-neighbor graphs](k-nearest-neighbor-graphs.qmd): the latter decides local neighborhoods, and Louvain partitions the resulting graph. It differs from [k-means and k-medoids](k-means-and-k-medoids-clustering.qmd), which directly optimize feature-space prototypes, and from [hierarchical clustering](hierarchical-clustering.qmd), which builds a linkage tree. The later [Leiden algorithm](leiden-community-detection.qmd) retains a multilevel modularity-style approach but adds refinement designed to avoid internally disconnected communities.

# Take-home Messages

1. Louvain greedily optimizes modularity through local vertex moves and graph aggregation.
2. The returned communities depend on the graph, null model, resolution, randomization, and optimization path.
3. In omics, validate labels against technical covariates, replication, markers, and stability—not a two-dimensional plot alone.
4. Louvain is scalable and useful, but its resolution limit and potentially disconnected communities motivate methods such as Leiden.
